cards.explanation: The answer is Show some sense. Bildad says, "Show some sense, and then we can talk." (Job 18:2) That's the whole ask, and he puts it up front like a bouncer at the door. I think Job heard it as a pretty big "first," friends. Bildad is Job's friend, and he starts with a push.

The answer is Stupid. Bildad asks, "Why are we regarded as cattle, as stupid in your sight?" (Job 18:3) So the word is stupid, friends. I think that question stung him, and it seems to carry into the rest of his speech.

The answer is the rocks moved from their place. Bildad asks, "…should the earth be forsaken on your account, or the rocks be moved from their place?" (Job 18:4) Two big questions, back to back. He's talking to Job, whom he calls someone who tears himself in anger. Rocks are about as stay-put as it gets, so I think he's making a point.

The answer is that it goes out. Bildad says, "…the lamp of the wicked is extinguished…" (Job 18:5) Then he says, "…the lamp beside him goes out." (Job 18:6) Same picture, said twice, bakers. A lamp that goes out leaves a tent dark, and that's the image he wants.

The answer is False. There are no enemies in this verse. Bildad says, "For his own feet lead him into a net, and he wanders into its mesh." (Job 18:8) His own feet take him there, and he wanders in. Bildad tells it as a man walking himself into trouble.

The answer is False, friends. Bildad says, "Terrors frighten him on every side and harass his every step." (Job 18:11) Every side, every step, no break. He pictures a man who can't find a calm spot anywhere.

The answer is the king of terrors. Bildad says the wicked man "…is torn from the shelter of his tent and is marched off to the king of terrors." (Job 18:14) That's a heavy title, friends, and it's the end of the road in his picture. I think this is one of his darkest lines.

The answers are roots and branches. Bildad says, "The roots beneath him dry up…" (Job 18:16) Then he says, "…the branches above him wither away." (Job 18:16) Roots dry up below and branches wither above, bakers, so Bildad moves from fire to a picture of a plant.

The answer is True. Bildad says, "The memory of him perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the land." (Job 18:17) Being forgotten is part of his picture, friends. It's a sad line, and I think it hits hard.

The answer is False. Bildad says, "He has no offspring or posterity among his people, no survivor where he once lived." (Job 18:19) So no offspring or posterity among his people, and no survivor where he once lived, friends. That's how he finishes the picture of the man's name fading out.

The answer is one who does not know God. Bildad ends with, "Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God." (Job 18:21) That's his closing line, bakers. He ties the dwelling of the wicked to the one who does not know God.
